'''New Brunswick''' has had, since the Legislative Council was abolished by an act passed on 16 April 1891,<ref name=cyb>[http://www65.statcan.gc.ca/acyb07/acyb07_2015b-eng.htm statcan.gc.ca: "Canada Year Book - Local Government of Canada, 1915 — New Brunswick"]</ref> a [[unicameral]] legislature called the [[New Brunswick Legislature]], consisting of the Lieutenant Governor and the [[Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick|Legislative Assembly]] with 49 seats. The legislature functions according to the [[Westminster system]] of government.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Desserud|first1=Donald|last2=Hyson|first2=Stewart|date=May 2012|title=New Brunswick's Legislative Assembly|url=http://www.revparlcan.ca/en/vol35-no1-new-brunswicks-legislative-assembly-donald-desserud-stewart-hyson-2/|journal=Canadian Parliamentary Review|volume=35|issue=1}}</ref> Elections are now held at least every five years but may be called at any time by the [[lieutenant governor]] (the vice-regal representative) on consultation with the [[premier]].

There are two dominant political parties in [[New Brunswick]], the [[Liberal Party of New Brunswick|Liberal Party]] and the [[Progressive Conservative Party of New Brunswick|Progressive Conservative Party]].<ref name=":0" /> From time to time, other parties such as the [[New Democratic Party of New Brunswick|New Democratic Party]], the [[Confederation of Regions Party]], and more recently, the [[Green Party of New Brunswick]] and [[People's Alliance of New Brunswick]] have held seats in the Legislative Assembly.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Quick facts about the four New Brunswick party leaders ahead of Sept. 14 election  {{!}} Globalnews.ca |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/7282399/quick-facts-about-the-four-new-brunswick-party-leaders-ahead-of-sept-14-election/ |access-date=2026-08-10 |work=Global News |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Political parties ==
{{See also|List of political parties in New Brunswick}}The two major political parties in New Brunswick are the [[New Brunswick Liberal Association]] and the [[Progressive Conservative Party of New Brunswick]].<ref name=":0" />

The [[United Farmers of New Brunswick|United Farmers]] earned 6 seats during the 1920 election.<ref name=":0" /> The [[New Brunswick Confederation of Regions Party|Confederation of Regions Party]] is the only minor party to have been official opposition at the [[Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick|legislative assembly]].<ref name=":0" /> It won 8 seats in the 1991 elections and 3 seats in 1995.<ref name=":0" />

The registered political parties during the 2024 elections are:<ref>{{Cite web|year=2021|title=Report of the Chief Electoral Officer - Fortieth General Provincial Election - September 14, 2020|url=https://www.electionsnb.ca/content/dam/enb/pdf/2020-prov-rpt.pdf|access-date=July 25, 2021|website=Elections NB}}</ref>

== Electoral system ==
{{Expand section|date=July 2021|small=no}}During the 1861 provincial elections, New Brunswick was the first in North America to use the secret ballot.<ref name=":0" />

In 1785, women were banned from voting by the [[Legislative Council of New Brunswick]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Elections |date=2021-04-06 |title=Chapter 2 – A History of the Vote in Canada |url=https://www.elections.ca/content.aspx?section=res&dir=his/chap2&document=index&lang=e#ftn6 |access-date=2022-07-06 |website=www.elections.ca}}</ref>  Women got the right to vote in provincial elections in 1919 and were allowed to be candidates in 1934.<ref name=":1" /> [[Brenda Robertson]] was the first woman elected to the legislative assembly during the 1967 provincial election.<ref name=":0" />

The Elections Act of 1952 prevented First Nations members to vote in provincial elections. This measure was revoked 11 years later.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Elections |first=New Brunswick |date=2014-02-03 |title=New Brunswick Election History - Elections NB |url=https://www.electionsnb.ca/content/enb/en/about-us/history.html |access-date=2022-07-06 |website=www.electionsnb.ca |language=en}}</ref>

Provincial elections occur every four years on the third Monday in October.<ref>{{Cite web|date=December 30, 2014|title=Legislative Assembly Act|url=http://laws.gnb.ca/en/showfulldoc/cs/2014-c.116//20210725|access-date=July 25, 2021}}</ref> New Brunswick first passed legislation to set a fixed election date in 2007.<ref name=":0"/>

==Elections==
{{see also|List of post-confederation New Brunswick general elections}}

===1867-1930===
From 1867 to 1878, party labels were not in use for general elections. While party identification began to be employed in the 1882 general election, parties did not become formally organized until the 1917 election, and were not legally recognized until 1935.

The financial condition of the county municipalities of the province was deemed excellent in 1915.  The ordinary revenue for the province in 1915 amounted to $1,634,079 and the ordinary expenditure to $1,626,634.  Findings were that ten counties out of fifteen (not including the city and county of [[Saint John, New Brunswick|Saint John]]) had an assessable valuation of real and personal property of over thirty million dollars, with insignificant liabilities.  The city of Saint John was in 1915 the commercial capital of the province, with a population of about 58,000, out of more than 350,000, in other words more than 16% of the total. Its valuation for assessment purposes in 1915 was $36,187,000 and its liabilities were less than $5,000,000. The city of Fredericton, the capital of the province, with a population in 1915 of 8,000, had a valuation of real and personal property for assessment of $5,000,000 with an outstanding indebtedness of $486,000.<ref name="cyb" />

===1935-1982===
Between 1935 and 1974, some ridings were [[Plurality-at-large voting|multi member]] seats – i.e., more than one [[Member of the Legislative Assembly]] was elected from certain ridings. Since 1974, each [[Electoral district (Canada)|riding]] (electoral district) has elected only [[First-past-the-post|one member]] to the [[Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick]].

===1987-present===
During the 1987 election, [[Frank McKenna]]'s liberal party won all 58 seats.<ref name=":0" /> 

Since 2000, the province has had six leaders, [[Bernard Lord]], [[Shawn Graham]], [[David Alward]], [[Brian Gallant]], [[Blaine Higgs]] and [[Susan Holt]].  The Canadian Broadcasting corporation characterized the policy differences between the parties as small.<ref>{{cite news |date=7 September 2006 |title=Dull debate won't sway any voters: analyst |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/dull-debate-won-t-sway-any-voters-analyst-1.605051 |work=[[CBC News]] |access-date=2 May 2026}}
</ref>

On September 19, 2006, the Liberals won a majority with 29 out of 55 seats, making 38-year-old [[Shawn Graham]] the new Premier of New Brunswick on a platform called the ''Charter for Change'', which pledged to focus on "the three Es": energy, education and the economy.<ref>{{Cite web| url= https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/liberals-topple-lord-s-tories-in-new-brunswick-1.609194| title=Liberals topple Lord's Tories in New Brunswick | website = CBC News | author-link= Canadian Broadcasting Corporation |date=September 2006 | access-date= 2007-02-15}}</ref>

In the [[2010 New Brunswick general election|2010 general election]], the Progressive Conservatives won 42 out of 55 seats, making [[David Alward]] the 32nd Premier of New Brunswick.<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/alward-faces-tough-challenges-after-n-b-win-1.931735|title= Alward faces tough challenges after N.B. win | website = Canadian Broadcasting Corporation |date=September 2010 | access-date= 2011-02-12}}</ref> The controversy this time was over [[Shawn Graham#Fourth year .282009.E2.80.9310.29|the planned sale of NB Power to Hydro-Québec]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bourque |first=Angelle |url=https://dalspace.library.dal.ca/bitstream/handle/10222/14251/BourqueAngelle_MA_POLISCI_Aug_2011.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |title=NB Power and Historical Institutionalism: Why the People of New Brunswick Could Not Accept the Sale |date=2011 |publisher=Dalhousie University |pages=28–29}}</ref>

On 24 September 2014 Brian Gallant was elected [[2014 New Brunswick general election|with 27 seats out of 49]].<ref name=GNbio>{{cite news|last1=Tucker|first1=Erika|title=Who is New Brunswick Premier-designate Brian Gallant?|url=http://globalnews.ca/news/1578233/who-is-new-brunswick-premier-designate-brian-gallant/|access-date=24 September 2014|publisher=Global News|date=23 September 2014}}</ref> An important election issue was [[hydraulic fracturing]], which was supported by the government, while the Liberal opposition promised to implement a moratorium on the practice.<ref name="Logan">{{cite news|last1=Logan|first1=Nick|title=N.B. election: Did shale gas and fracking sway the vote?|url=http://globalnews.ca/news/1577434/|access-date=10 June 2016|agency=Global News New Brunswick|date=23 September 2014}}</ref><ref name="Annis">{{cite news|last1=Annis|first1=Roger|title=Pro-gas fracking government turfed in New Brunswick election|url=http://www.vancouverobserver.com/world/canada/pro-gas-fracking-government-turfed-new-brunswick-election|access-date=10 June 2016|work=Vancouver Observer|date=24 September 2014}}</ref> As [[Green Party of New Brunswick]] elected with their first seat for their leader [[David Coon]] in newly created [[Fredericton South]] district.

On [[2018 New Brunswick general election|24 September 2018]], the Progressive Conservatives won 22 out of 49 seats, while the Liberal party received the plurality of votes cast. The Liberals won 21 seats. The Green Party of New Brunswick and the [[People's Alliance of New Brunswick]] each won 3 seats.

On [[2020 New Brunswick general election|14 September 2020]], the Progressive Conservatives won 27 out of 49 seats, thus getting a small PC majority, while the Liberal party decreasing both voters and losing 4 seats. The Green Party of New Brunswick retains its 3 seats, but gaining more voters. While, the People's Alliance of New Brunswick has loss more voters than the Liberals, and lose one seat.

On [[2024 New Brunswick general election|21 September 2024]], the Liberals gained a decisive majority of 31, wilth the Progressive Conservatives and Greens winning 16 and 2 respectively.

== Political culture and issues ==
The dynamics of New Brunswick politics differ from those of other provinces in Canada. The lack of a dominant urban centre in the province means that the government has to be responsive to issues affecting all areas of the province.<ref>{{Cite news |website=CBC News New Brunswick |date=2010 |title=A new deal for N.B.'s largest cities |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/a-new-deal-for-n-b-s-largest-cities-1.880129 |access-date=June 23, 2024}}</ref> In addition, the presence of a large francophone minority plays a large role in political decision making in the province.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Canadian Parliamentary Review - Article |url=http://www.revparl.ca/english/issue.asp?param=133&art=852 |access-date=2024-06-23 |website=www.revparl.ca}}</ref>

From 1960 until the appointment of [[Blaine Higgs]] in 2018,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Moore |first1=Nick |title=New Brunswick premier says being unilingual in a bilingual province makes him 'a target' |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/atlantic/article/new-brunswick-premier-says-being-unilingual-in-a-bilingual-province-makes-him-a-target/ |access-date=June 23, 2024 |work=[[CTV Atlantic]] |date=December 13, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> the province has generally elected young bilingual leaders.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-11-02 |title=Brian Gallant joins long list of young former New Brunswick premiers |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/atlantic/article/brian-gallant-joins-long-list-of-young-former-new-brunswick-premiers/ |access-date=2024-06-23 |website=Atlantic |language=en}}</ref> As bilingualism is an unofficial pre-requisite for major party leaders in Canadian federal government, this combination of attributes sometimes contributes to speculation the premiers of New Brunswick to become federal leaders.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-01-22 |title=Opinion: Want to be a federal leader in Canada? Speak both official languages |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/article-want-to-be-a-federal-leader-in-canada-speak-both-official-languages/ |access-date=2024-06-23 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref> Former Premier [[Bernard Lord]] (Progressive Conservative) has been touted as a potential leader of the [[Conservative Party of Canada]]. [[Frank McKenna]] (premier, 1987–1997), had been considered to be a front-runner to succeed Prime Minister [[Paul Martin]].
